\subsection{Uncalibrated Simulation}\label{sec:sim}

The simulator asks two questions: does a simulation that satisfies a
proposition's assumptions reproduce its closed form, and when an
assumption is dropped, does the decision the proposition implies
survive? It is not calibrated. Its parameters are illustrative, every
number is a property of the simulated model under its workload, and
none is a measurement of a serving system. \texttt{libqueuingsim} is an
event-driven simulator in Rust whose two-resource replica runs
iterations of length $\max(\omega+\beta K_B,\ n\,a)$ for a batch of $n$
decoding turns holding $K_B$ tokens of KV, so decode is a bandwidth PS
with the demand~\eqref{eq:decode} and prefill is a FIFO server that
receives the compute the batch leaves; resident KV is a prefix, and a
turn re-prefills what was evicted with the work~\eqref{eq:prefill}.
Unless stated, $a=2\cdot10^{-5}$, $b=2\cdot10^{-9}$,
$\omega=2\cdot10^{-4}$ and $\beta=2\cdot10^{-9}$ seconds per token.
Each proposition is a named check with fixed seeds and an explicit
tolerance; of \simChecks{} checks, \simChecksPassed{} pass. Confidence
intervals are 95\,\% batch means or, where stated, across independent
seeds; the best value in each comparison is in bold.
Appendix~\ref{app:sim} holds the tables summarised below.

\input{sim/tab-inmodel}

\paragraph{In model.} Table~\ref{tab:sim-inmodel} compares the closed
forms with simulation under their own assumptions: the M/M/1 response
time, the PK wait, the variance ratio, the $(1+\mathrm{CV}^2)/2$ ratio
and the worst shortest-first ratio over 9000 instances agree with
theory within the confidence interval or 2\,\%, and forcing misses on a
fraction $\delta$ of turns at an M/G/1 server raises the number of turns
by an amount inside the bracket of Proposition~\ref{prop:price}, at its
upper end where the exact PK difference lies. On the two-resource
replica the same forced misses raise the prefill queue inside the
bracket and leave the decode batch unchanged, as
Proposition~\ref{prop:decode} says; under PS, deterministic and hit/miss
work of equal mean give the same occupancy while a FIFO server
separates them (Table~\ref{tab:sim-ps}). These checks confirm the
simulator, not the propositions.

\paragraph{Beyond the model.} Four assumptions are dropped in turn.
\emph{A real batch cap} (Table~\ref{tab:sim-lps},
Figure~\ref{fig:sim-lps}): the saturating $\varphi$ agrees with an exact
cap of eight within 1\,\% at half load, and at high load its error
follows the work $\mathrm{CV}^2$, holding 22\,\% too many turns for
deterministic work and 51\,\% too few for $\mathrm{CV}^2=4$, so the
model underestimates decode congestion at a capped replica near
saturation. \emph{Eviction offline} (Table~\ref{tab:sim-evict},
Figure~\ref{fig:sim-evict}): against the exact optimum on random
instances, shortest-first and price-per-byte order coincide when the
$p_i$ are equal and stay within a factor of two, as
Proposition~\ref{prop:blind}(ii) requires; when $p_i$ varies,
shortest-first reaches ten times the optimum, price-per-byte order
stays close, and the guarded greedy is within $1.9$ of the optimum on
every instance. \emph{Open sessions} (Tables~\ref{tab:sim-evict-dyn}
and~\ref{tab:sim-admission}, Figure~\ref{fig:sim-admission}): with
Poisson sessions of two synthetic classes on a 600k-token pool, the
price is paid in TTFT, whose p99 is ten to seventeen times its mean
because up to eight prefills queue behind a document miss while turn
response exceeds TTFT by a constant decode time; the priced rules,
which here take $p_i$ and $\tau_i$ from the generating class, have the
lowest TTFT in most cells but no cell separates them from shortest-first
beyond the seed noise, while LRU is worst everywhere; and admission
decides more than the eviction order, since with at most 16 live
sessions the hit rate stays at $0.99$ at both loads while with 32 most
seeds thrash at the higher load. \emph{Placement}
(Table~\ref{tab:sim-inversion}): over four replicas with a skewed
placement and a state moved over one shared link, the load at which
always moving beats affinity rises as the link slows, as
\eqref{eq:rhostar} says; the affinity node's utilisation at the
inversion is $0.19$ against $\rho^*=0.25$ for a link that moves a
context in a few tens of milliseconds, and for a link slower than a
recompute the inversion comes only once the affinity node saturates,
with the link itself $97\,\%$ busy, a shared resource the single-node
formula does not see. The lookahead rule of~\eqref{eq:lookahead} is
below both at every load.

\paragraph{Replayed production sessions.} Table~\ref{tab:sim-trace}
replaces the synthetic classes by the production sessions of
\S\ref{sec:exp-traces}: each session replays a real session's appends,
outputs, think times and length, so the workload side of the model is
measured and only the replica is simulated. A gap above ten minutes
starts a new session, whose first prompt is the whole accumulated
context (median \wkFirstCtxSplit k tokens against \wkFirstCtxNew k for
a genuinely new session; \wkSplitShare\,\% of replayed sessions start
this way); splitting at thirty minutes instead changes the corpus but
leaves the open-pool row within seed noise
(Table~\ref{tab:sim-trace-split}). The cost model uses
$b=4\cdot10^{-10}$, so that attention overtakes the dense term at
$50$k tokens, since the contexts are ten times longer than the
synthetic ones. Three things follow. First, with no eviction every
follow-up turn hits and the prefill work of follow-up turns still has
$\mathrm{CV}^2=\simTraceOpenCvMin$--$\simTraceOpenCvMax$, from the
appends alone; the mean TTFT of
\simTraceOpenTtftMin--\simTraceOpenTtftMax\,s is set by the cold first
prompts, which every turn behind them waits for. Second, once the pool
is finite the cap on live sessions binds throughout the run, the
replica is a closed system of $N$ sessions and the entry queue grows
for the whole horizon (up to \simTraceEntryMaxHours{} hours of mean
wait). At the tight cap the hit rate stays at or above
\simTraceTightHitMin{} and the hit/miss mixture supplies
\simTraceTightMixMin--\simTraceTightMixMax\,\% of the variance of
follow-up prefill work, the simulated version of the split of
Table~\ref{tab:cv2} once eviction is active; at the loose cap the
replica thrashes, the hit rate falls to at most \simTraceLooseHitMax{}
and the mean TTFT exceeds \simTraceLooseTtftMin\,s. Third, the PK wait
computed from the measured $\lambda$, $\E[S]$ and $\E[S^2]$ of the
prefill queue is above the observed wait in every cell, by a factor of
\simTracePkRatioMin{} to \simTracePkRatioMax; the largest factors are in
the cells with $\rho$ near one, where the open formula is near its pole,
but the direction holds at $\rho=0.25$ with five sessions live, as
Proposition~\ref{prop:finite} says it must for exponential work. For
the price itself, Table~\ref{tab:sim-trace-price} forces a share
$\delta$ of resident follow-up turns to miss with no pool limit and
compares the rise of the number in the prefill stage with the bracket
of Proposition~\ref{prop:price} from the baseline's measured moments.
At $\delta\le3\,\%$, with \simPriceLiveMin{} to \simPriceLiveMax{}
sessions live, the observed rise is \simPriceSmallRatioMin{} to
\simPriceSmallRatioMax{} of the bracket's lower end, so the open price
overstates the cost of a few misses, as the finite population predicts;
at $\delta=10\,\%$ the observed rise is \simPriceLargeRatioMin{} to
\simPriceLargeRatioMax{} times the lower end and the upper end
diverges, because the added load puts the open queue near its pole
while the closed system saturates gracefully, and because the misses of
long-context sessions lengthen the sessions themselves, which the
stationary price does not count. The open price is therefore a bound
for a few misses and not for many, and E2 has to report the number of
live sessions next to the load.

\paragraph{What the simulation does not show.} The simulator shares
the model's abstractions: no block-level KV allocation beyond tail
blocks, no partial prefix hits across sessions, no collective
contention, one capacity function for prefill and decode, and
parameters chosen to be plausible, not measured. Its results say which
decisions are robust to the assumptions we dropped, not how often each
regime occurs in practice.
